title: 5 Solo Pool Drills to Improve Fast (20 Minutes a Day)
description: No partner needed. Try these five simple pool drills to sharpen your aim, stroke and cue ball control in just 20 minutes.
body:
Want to get better at pool without a coach, a league or an opponent? Good news: you only need a table, a rack of balls and about 20 minutes. The players you watch at the Mosconi Cup did not get that good by only playing matches. They put in hours of simple, repeatable practice. Here are five solo drills that anyone can try this week.

Why drills beat just playing games

In a normal game you hit a shot, get a different layout and rarely see the same shot twice. Drills flip that. You repeat one skill again and again, so your stroke and your eyes learn what "right" feels like. Keep a quick tally of how many you make and try to beat your own score next time.

Drill 1: The straight-in stop shot

Place an object ball a hand-width or two in front of a corner pocket, then put the cue ball straight back from it so the shot is dead straight. Hit the cue ball with center-ball contact and a smooth stroke. Your goals are simple: make the ball and have the cue ball stop dead where the object ball was.

  • Start close together, then move the cue ball farther back as you improve.
  • Count how many out of 10 you pocket and stop.
  • If the cue ball keeps rolling forward, your stroke is likely too hard or you are hitting above center.

Drill 2: The down-the-table stroke check

Place the cue ball on the head spot and hit it softly up the middle of the table, aiming for it to come straight back to your tip. A straight stroke sends the ball back along the same line. If it drifts to one side, your cue is swinging off line. This is a great warm-up and it costs you nothing but a few minutes.

Drill 3: The cut shot ladder

Set an object ball near a pocket and the cue ball a few diamonds away. Start with an easy slight cut and, after you make a few, move the cue ball to create a slightly bigger angle. Keep climbing the ladder until the cut becomes hard. You will quickly learn which angles you trust and which ones need work. Pay attention to where you aim, since beginners often cut the ball too thin on big angles.

Drill 4: Speed control to the rail

Pocketing balls is only half of pool. The other half is where the cue ball ends up. Try shooting the cue ball from one end of the table and stopping it softly against the far cushion, then try to stop it just short of the cushion. Next, try to roll it to a chosen spot, such as a diamond on the side rail. Good speed control makes position play so much easier later on.

Drill 5: Three-ball run-out

Scatter three balls around the table, with no balls close to the rails if you are a beginner. Your job is to pocket all three in order, using the cue ball to set up each next shot. Once that feels comfortable, move up to four, five or the whole rack. This is the drill that connects everything: aiming, speed and planning. It also mirrors what pros do when they are trying to run out a rack.

Make your practice stick

  • Warm up first. Hit a few easy shots before you start counting scores.
  • Chalk up every shot. It is a small habit with a big effect on avoiding miscues.
  • Keep it short. Twenty focused minutes beats two sloppy hours.
  • Write it down. A tiny notebook of your scores shows real progress.

A simple weekly plan

If you are not sure how to fit all this in, try a three-day rhythm. On day one, spend your time on the stop shot and the stroke check, because straight shots build the foundation for everything else. On day two, work on the cut shot ladder and speed control. On day three, finish with the three-ball run-out and then play a relaxed game for fun. Repeating the cycle for a few weeks usually makes shots that once felt hard start to feel natural.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Rushing the stroke. Pause at the end of your backswing and keep your head still until the ball is gone.
  • Hitting too hard. Most drills work best at a medium or soft pace, and control matters more than power.
  • Skipping the plan. Decide where the cue ball should stop before you shoot, not after.
  • Quitting after a bad run. Missing is how you learn. Reset the balls and go again.

Take it to a real event

Once your drills start paying off, test your skills. Browse upcoming tournaments near you, check the events calendar, or look at what is happening this weekend. Want to watch the best in the world? The Mosconi Cup runs November 27-30 at the Caribe Royale Resort in Orlando, and our Mosconi Cup 2026 hub has the dates and how to follow along. More basics live in our pool guides.

Your turn

Pick one drill, give it ten minutes at your next session and track your score. Then come back to the next one. Small, repeated practice is how every great player started. Which drill will you try first?
